Interface LogProperty.Result<T>

Type Parameters:
T - property type.
All Known Subinterfaces:
LogProperty.RequiredResult<T>, LogProperty.Result.Success<T>, LogProperty.ValidatedResult<T>
All Known Implementing Classes:
LogProperty.Result.Error, LogProperty.Result.Missing
Enclosing interface:

The result of a property fetched from properties.

  • Method Details

    • validate

      default LogProperty.ValidatedResult<T> validate(LogProperty.Validator validator)
      Registers this result with validator via LogProperty.Validator.add(Result) (a still-LogProperty.Result.Missing result is treated as a real failure) and returns this result unchanged, so a chain that builds a required property can register itself with a shared LogProperty.Validator and keep going in one expression - properties.forKey(key).ofString().or(fallback).validate(v) - instead of a separate var x = ...; v.add(x); statement pair. The validator is shared and single-use by design: add every property's result this way (or via validateIfError(Validator) for an optional one), then call LogProperty.Validator.validate() exactly once at the end to report every failure together instead of one exception per property.
      Parameters:
      validator - validator to add this result to.
      Returns:
      this result, unchanged.

    • validateIfError

      default LogProperty.ValidatedResult<T> validateIfError(LogProperty.Validator validator)
      Like validate(Validator) but via LogProperty.Validator.addIfError(Result) instead of LogProperty.Validator.add(Result) - a LogProperty.Result.Missing result is expected and ignored, only a LogProperty.Result.Error is treated as a failure. Intended for an optional property that already has a fallback applied (for example via or(Object)): the property being absent is fine, but if it was present and failed to convert that should not be swallowed.
      Parameters:
      validator - validator to add this result to.
      Returns:
      this result, unchanged.

    • validateNow

      default T validateNow(Class<?> component)
      Convenience for a genuine one-off, single-property validation that does not need to participate in a larger batch: builds a single-use LogProperty.Validator, registers this result with it via LogProperty.Validator.add(Result), and validates immediately - instead of registering with a caller-managed LogProperty.Validator via validate(Validator) and deferring to a later LogProperty.Validator.validate() call.

      Uses LogProperty.Validator.add(Result) semantics: a still-LogProperty.Result.Missing result is treated as a failure, same as an absent required property with no fallback. If this property is optional, apply a fallback first - properties.forKey(key).ofString().or(fallback).validateNow(component) - since a result with a fallback applied is never LogProperty.Result.Missing. For a property that should tolerate being missing but not being present-and-malformed, use validateIfError(Validator) with an externally-owned LogProperty.Validator instead - there is deliberately no addIfError-equivalent of this method, to avoid two same-named single-property convenience methods with silently different failure semantics.

      Parameters:
      component - the class on whose behalf this property is being resolved - only used to name the source of the failure in the exception message.
      Returns:
      value.
      Throws:
      LogProperty.ValidationException - if this result is not a LogProperty.Result.Success.

    • map

      <U> LogProperty.Result<U> map(LogProperty.PropertyFunction<T, U, ? super Exception> mapper)
      Maps this result's value through mapper. On success, keeps the origin (topProperties/properties/key/ rawValue/kind, see PropertySuccess) so a later conversion step's error message can still point back to it. On failure, builds a rich error message - which key it came from, where that key was found, and (for LogProperty.PropertyConvertException/LogProperty.ValidationException causes) the original raw value - with a "Tried:" line searching topProperties: the LogProperties the very first LogProperties.forKey(String) in this chain was looked up against, which for a chained/composite LogProperties.of(a, b) can be broader than the exact source the value was actually found at. Usable at any point in a chain, not just directly off a LogProperty, since a LogProperty.Result.Success keeps pointing back to the property it originally came from no matter how many conversions have run since.
      Type Parameters:
      U - result type
      Parameters:
      mapper - mapping function.
      Returns:
      mapped result.
